papers.title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety lies at the core of developing and deploying large language models (LLMs). However, previous safety benchmarks only concern the safety in one language, e.g. the majority language in the pretraining data such as English. In this work, we build the first multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs, XSafety, in response to the global deployment of LLMs in practice. XSafety covers 14 kinds of commonly used safety issues across 10 languages that span several language families. We utilize XSafety to empirically study the multilingual safety for 4 widely-used LLMs, including both close-API and open-source models. Experimental results show that all LLMs produce significantly more unsafe responses for non-English queries than English ones, indicating the necessity of developing safety alignment for non-English languages. In addition, we propose several simple and effective prompting methods to improve the multilingual safety of ChatGPT by evoking safety knowledge and improving cross-lingual generalization of safety alignment. Our prompting method can significantly reduce the ratio of unsafe responses from 19.1% to 9.7% for non-English queries. We release our data at https://github.com/Jarviswang94/Multilingual_safety_benchmark.

papers.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularity of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, a growing amount of attention is paid to their safety concerns. These models may generate insulting and discriminatory content, reflect incorrect social values, and may be used for malicious purposes such as fraud and dissemination of misleading information. Evaluating and enhancing their safety is particularly essential for the wide application of large language models (LLMs). To further promote the safe deployment of LLMs, we develop a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark. Our benchmark explores the comprehensive safety performance of LLMs from two perspectives: 8 kinds of typical safety scenarios and 6 types of more challenging instruction attacks. Our benchmark is based on a straightforward process in which it provides the test prompts and evaluates the safety of the generated responses from the evaluated model. In evaluation, we utilize the LLM's strong evaluation ability and develop it as a safety evaluator by prompting. On top of this benchmark, we conduct safety assessments and analyze 15 LLMs including the OpenAI GPT series and other well-known Chinese LLMs, where we observe some interesting findings. For example, we find that instruction attacks are more likely to expose safety issues of all LLMs. Moreover, to promote the development and deployment of safe, responsible, and ethical AI, we publicly release SafetyPrompts including 100k augmented prompts and responses by LLMs.

papers.title: Safety at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Model and Agent Safety
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large models, driven by their exceptional abilities in learning and generalization through large-scale pre-training, has reshaped the landscape of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These models are now foundational to a wide range of applications, including conversational AI, recommendation systems, autonomous driving, content generation, medical diagnostics, and scientific discovery. However, their widespread deployment also exposes them to significant safety risks, raising concerns about robustness, reliability, and ethical implications. This survey provides a systematic review of current safety research on large models, covering Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and large-model-powered Agents. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive taxonomy of safety threats to these models, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, energy-latency attacks, data and model extraction attacks, and emerging agent-specific threats. (2) We review defense strategies proposed for each type of attacks if available and summarize the commonly used datasets and benchmarks for safety research. (3) Building on this, we identify and discuss the open challenges in large model safety, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, scalable and effective defense mechanisms, and sustainable data practices. More importantly, we highlight the necessity of collective efforts from the research community and international collaboration. Our work can serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners, fostering the ongoing development of comprehensive defense systems and platforms to safeguard AI models.

papers.title: Enhanced Diagnostic and Interpretable Model for Febrile Diseases Using Explainable AI and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: <p><span>Tropical febrile diseases pose significant public health challenges in tropical regions, particularly in resource-limited settings, where timely and accurate diagnoses are critical for effective disease management. However, existing diagnostic systems are black-box and often lack interpretability, making it difficult for healthcare practitioners to understand and trust machine learning (ML) predictions. Additionally, the existing system excludes younger patients, limiting its applicability. This study aimed to develop an integrated diagnostic system that enhances interpretability by leveraging machine learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), and a large language model (LLM). A dataset comprising 3,914 patient records with 32 symptoms was obtained from a New Frontiers in Research Fund-sponsored project and preprocessed for analysis. Random Forest (RF) was trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation to optimize its performance. The tuned model achieved high diagnostic performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing six febrile diseases. To enhance interpretability, a Model Interpretability Framework (MIF) was incorporated, integrating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for visual insights and ChatGPT for textual explanations. This combination provided users with a clear understanding of the diagnostic process, addressing the limitations of black-box ML models. The system was implemented using Python in a development environment that included Google Colaboratory, Visual Studio Code, Flet, and MySQL for database management. Agile development methodology and Unified Modeling Language tools were employed to create a user-friendly design for clinicians and patients. The diagnostic system was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. The RF model achieved outstanding precision for most diseases, high recall (≥0.97), and an AUC-ROC of 0.99, indicating nearly flawless training performance with few misclassifications. On the test dataset, the model performed better in diagnosing malaria (F1-score = 88%, precision = 85%), urinary tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 80%), and respiratory tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 77%). The evaluated system demonstrated strong predictive performance, correctly identifying 72 out of 99 tested patient cases, with 26 cases misclassified and one case completely missed. It achieved the highest detection rates for Malaria and HIV/AIDS, accurately identifying all cases without false positives. This work enhances diagnostic solutions for tropical healthcare settings by improving explainability and ensuring inclusivity for younger patients, addressing key limitations in existing systems. The integration of ML, XAI, and LLM enhances diagnostic performance and lays the groundwork for future AI-driven healthcare innovations, ultimately improving health outcomes in resource-scarce regions. Healthcare providers should adopt this system to enhance the efficiency of disease diagnosis and extend the system to diagnose additional medical conditions.&nbsp;</span></p>

literature_themes.theme: Safety Assessment of Large Language Models Across Languages
literature_themes.summary: This cluster of papers focuses on the safety of large language models (LLMs) in multilingual contexts, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety benchmarks that address safety issues in multiple languages. It highlights the disparity in safety performance between English and non-English queries and proposes methods to enhance safety alignment in LLMs. Additionally, it surveys safety threats and defenses related to various large AI models, providing a broad overview of safety concerns in the field.
literature_themes.limitations: The studies primarily focus on specific languages (e.g., Chinese and English) and may not fully address the safety challenges in less-represented languages. There is also a need for more extensive evaluation of safety benchmarks across diverse applications and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, the effectiveness of proposed prompting methods may vary across different LLM architectures.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster identifies critical gaps in the safety assessment of LLMs, particularly in non-English languages, and underscores the necessity for multilingual safety benchmarks. It supports research gap identification by highlighting the need for improved safety measures and evaluation frameworks that can be generalized across various languages and applications.

literature_themes.summary: This cluster primarily investigates the integration of large language models to improve the performance of few-shot recommender systems. It explores how enhanced representations can empower these systems to make better recommendations with limited data.
literature_themes.limitations: The cluster lacks comprehensive empirical validation across diverse datasets and contexts. Additionally, the absence of an abstract for one of the papers limits the understanding of its contributions and findings.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights the potential of leveraging advanced language models in recommendation systems, identifying a research gap in the application of such models in scenarios with sparse data, which can guide future studies in this area.

summary: Recent studies emphasize the importance of interpretable internal representations in large language models (LLMs) to enhance safety and controllability. Researchers propose methods to visualize and understand the decision-making processes of LLMs, aiming to reduce biases and improve transparency. Techniques such as attention visualization and layer-wise relevance propagation are explored to ensure that model outputs align with human values and ethical standards.
scholarly_positioning: While prior research has made strides in visualizing internal representations of large language models (LLMs) through techniques like attention visualization and layer-wise relevance propagation, these approaches often fall short in addressing the complex interplay between model interpretability and ethical alignment. Existing methods primarily focus on post-hoc analysis rather than integrating interpretability into the model design, leaving unresolved tensions regarding real-time safety and controllability. Furthermore, the lack of standardized metrics for evaluating interpretability hinders the ability to compare different approaches effectively. This proposed research aims to bridge these gaps by developing frameworks that not only enhance interpretability but also ensure that LLM outputs consistently reflect human values, thereby contributing to the broader discourse on ethical AI development.

research_scope: This study will focus on enhancing the interpretability of large language models (LLMs) specifically in the context of automated content moderation tasks. The target population will include various LLMs trained on diverse datasets, with a focus on their ability to generate outputs that align with ethical standards in content moderation. The evaluation period will span six months, during which the models will undergo benchmark evaluations and ablation studies to assess their interpretability and safety. A control group will consist of traditional LLMs without integrated interpretability frameworks. Primary outcomes will include the alignment of model outputs with predefined ethical guidelines, while secondary outcomes will assess user trust and satisfaction through human evaluations and output-level explanations.
concept_definition: 1. Large Language Models (LLMs): AI models trained on extensive textual data to generate human-like text. 2. Interpretability: The degree to which a model's internal workings can be understood, often assessed through methods like probing or attention visualization. 3. Internal Representations: Hidden states or activations within the model that capture information about input data, accessible through techniques like layer-wise relevance propagation. 4. Safety Outcomes: Metrics assessing the model's outputs for harmful content, including unsafe response rate (frequency of harmful outputs), over-refusal (excessive refusal to generate content), jailbreak success (ability to bypass safety measures), harmful compliance (generation of harmful content when prompted), and refusal precision/recall (accuracy of the model's refusals). 5. User Trust: The confidence users have in the model's outputs, characterized by trust calibration (alignment of user expectations with model performance), blind trust (unquestioning reliance on model outputs), perceived transparency (clarity of model decision-making), and appropriate reliance (using the model's outputs in suitable contexts). 6. Controllability: The ability to steer model outputs towards desired outcomes, often enhanced through interpretability frameworks. 7. Ethical Standards: Predefined guidelines that govern acceptable content generation, ensuring alignment with human values in automated content moderation tasks.
technical_feasibility: The study requires access to open-source LLMs or models with hidden-state extraction capabilities for analyzing internal representations. It also necessitates labeled datasets for evaluating safety outcomes and user trust, as well as multilingual prompt sets for diverse evaluations. Human participants are needed for trust calibration and satisfaction assessments, which will require ethics approval. GPU resources will be essential for running ablation studies and model evaluations. Annotation protocols must be established for consistent evaluation of outputs. If only API models are available, the design should shift towards output-level explanations and black-box evaluations. Missing resources include access to open-source models and labeled datasets. A feasible adjustment would be to focus on output-level explanations using available API models while conducting a comparative analysis with existing open-source models for interpretability assessments.
gap: Prior studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of attention visualization and layer-wise relevance propagation in enhancing interpretability in large language models (LLMs) within the context of ethical AI development; however, they treat the integration of interpretability into model design as secondary, leaving unclear whether real-time safety and controllability are affected by these interpretability frameworks; this matters practically because ensuring that LLM outputs consistently reflect human values is crucial for applications like automated content moderation; therefore, this study investigates the development of integrated interpretability frameworks that enhance both safety and controllability in LLMs within the defined scope.
question: How do integrated interpretability frameworks in large language models (LLMs) affect the alignment of generated outputs with ethical standards in automated content moderation compared to traditional LLMs without such frameworks?
theoretical_mechanism: In this research, the independent variable is the integrated interpretability frameworks implemented in large language models (LLMs). The mediator for system-level outcomes, such as unsafe response rate and refusal accuracy, is the enhanced representation features that improve safety detection and steering mechanisms. The moderator is the ethical standards that guide the alignment of model outputs. The dependent variable is the alignment of generated outputs with these ethical standards. For user-level outcomes, perceived transparency acts as a mediator between the model's interpretability and user satisfaction. The causal chain suggests that improved interpretability leads to better representation features, which in turn enhance safety outcomes and user trust. Assumptions requiring empirical validation include the effectiveness of interpretability frameworks in real-time scenarios and the direct influence of perceived transparency on user behavior and satisfaction.
hypothesis: Integrated interpretability frameworks in large language models (LLMs) will lead to a greater alignment of generated outputs with ethical standards in automated content moderation compared to traditional LLMs, mediated by enhanced representation features that improve safety detection.

methodology: This study will employ a benchmark evaluation framework to assess the impact of integrated interpretability frameworks on large language models (LLMs) in automated content moderation tasks. Participants will include various LLMs, with a control group consisting of traditional models lacking interpretability features. The primary operationalized variables will include alignment of outputs with ethical standards, measured through output classification metrics, and user trust, assessed via surveys and trust calibration logs. The evaluation will utilize ablation studies to isolate the effects of interpretability features on safety outcomes, such as unsafe response rates and refusal accuracy. To ensure validity, confounding variables such as variability in training data and user biases will be controlled through randomized sampling and consistent annotation protocols. The study will focus on English and include multilingual prompt sets to assess cross-linguistic performance, with native-speaker validation to mitigate translation biases. Reproducibility will be supported by detailed documentation of model configurations and evaluation procedures.

proposal: This research proposal aims to enhance the interpretability of large language models (LLMs) in automated content moderation by developing integrated interpretability frameworks that align model outputs with ethical standards. Key concepts include LLMs, interpretability (defined as the clarity of internal workings), internal representations (hidden states capturing input data), safety outcomes (metrics for harmful content detection), user trust (confidence in model outputs), controllability (steering outputs towards desired outcomes), and ethical standards (guidelines for acceptable content). The study assumes access to open-source LLMs, labeled datasets, and GPU resources for evaluations. Building on literature that highlights limitations in post-hoc interpretability methods, this research addresses the empirical gap regarding the integration of interpretability into model design for real-time safety and controllability, particularly in automated content moderation, where alignment with human values is critical. The central research question is: How do integrated interpretability frameworks in LLMs affect the alignment of generated outputs with ethical standards in automated content moderation compared to traditional LLMs? The theoretical mechanism posits that integrated interpretability frameworks (independent variable) enhance representation features (mediator), improving alignment with ethical standards (dependent variable) while perceived transparency mediates user trust (user-level outcome). The falsifiable hypothesis states that integrated interpretability frameworks will lead to greater alignment of outputs with ethical standards compared to traditional LLMs, mediated by enhanced representation features. Constructs will be operationalized using output classification metrics for alignment, probing accuracy for representation features, and surveys for user trust. The methodology will employ benchmark evaluations and ablation studies with a control group of traditional LLMs, ensuring validity through randomized sampling and consistent annotation protocols. Expected contributions include theoretical advancements in understanding the causal relationship between interpretability and ethical alignment, technical innovations in methodology for assessing interpretability, empirical evidence on the effectiveness of these frameworks, and practical guidelines for deploying LLMs in ethical contexts. Key limitations include potential confounding variables, variability in training data, and the risk of misinterpretation of negative results, necessitating robust confound control strategies and clear communication of findings.
